title: What Force Makes of Us
author: Jonathan Boymal
summary: Jonathan Boymal examines Simone Weil's 1940 essay on Homer's Iliad, arguing that her central insight - force is not a divine order but a power operating on persons - remains devastatingly current. Weil defines force as that which turns human beings into things, whether by killing or by extinguishing the will of the living. What makes her reading radical is its symmetry: force dehumanizes not only those subjected to it but those who wield it, intoxicating them and destroying the interval of reflection between impulse and action. Boymal traces Homer's depiction of victory as always temporary - circulating force operates as a plague without loyalty. The Iliad models an 'equity of suffering,' mourning Trojans and Greeks with equal tenderness, which Weil holds up as the literary form of compassionate attention to the other. Boymal closes by noting that this framework illuminates any institution where force operates without the check of reflection: the boardroom as much as the battlefield.
points: Weil defines force as that which turns any person subjected to it into a thing - most obviously through death but also through slavery and social invisibility - relocating force from a divine order to a feature of all power relationships.

The essay's most counterintuitive claim is that force is symmetrical: it crushes its victims but equally intoxicates its wielders, destroying the interval of reflection between impulse and action that is the space where both justice and humanity actually live.

Victory in the Iliad is always temporary - those who hold force 'on loan from fate count on it too much and are destroyed' - meaning no leader or institution should mistake current dominance for a stable condition.

Weil's 'equity of suffering' - Homer mourning Greeks and Trojans with equal tenderness - models a compassionate attention that she holds up against force as nearly a spiritual act and a literary ideal almost no other war narrative achieves.

Boymal extends Weil's framework beyond the battlefield: wherever force operates without the small interval of reflection - the boardroom, the institution, the classroom - the same dehumanizing dynamics unfold with the same regularity.
quotes: Force is as pitiless to the man who possesses it, or thinks he does, as it is to its victims; the second it crushes, the first it intoxicates.
The true hero, the true subject, the center of the Iliad is force. Force employed by man, force that enslaves man, force before which man's flesh shrinks away.
To define force - it is that x that turns anybody who is subjected to it into a thing. Exercised to the limit, it turns man into a thing in the most literal sense: it makes a corpse out of him.

The man who is the possessor of force seems to walk through a non-resistant element; in the human substance that surrounds him nothing has the power to interpose, between the impulse and the act, the tiny interval that is reflection. Where there is no room for reflection, there is none either for justice or prudence.
Those that have force on loan from fate count on it too much and are destroyed.

Weil's point is wherever force operates at scale, it transforms everyone it touches. It intoxicates those who hold it. It crushes those who don't. And it tends, with terrible regularity, to reverse itself.
She wrote that in 1940. It remains, unfortunately, true.
